extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, constructive mathematicians, and foundations researchers (graduate students and scholars interested in Bishop-style constructivism)
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly, philosophical examination of Errett Bishop’s constructive mathematics: its foundational assumptions, its differences from Brouwerian/intutionistic approaches, and implications for meaning, computation, and formalization. The piece aims to revive philosophical debate and suggest directions for a Bishop-inspired philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give numerical meaning to as much as possible of classical abstract analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our program is simple: to give numerical meaning to as much as possible of classical abstract analysis.” (Bishop) — constructive mathematics should endow classical statements with numerical (computational) interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a central programmematic criterion: when reformulating classical results constructively, one should supply explicit numerical/algorithmic content (witnesses, procedures). Statements or principles that do not admit a numerical interpretation are treated as defective for Bishop-style constructivism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive mathematics as predictive (finitely performable computations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive mathematics is 'predictive' in that it 'describes or predicts the result of certain finitely performable, albeit hypothetical, computations within the set of integers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret logical constants and quantifiers so they correspond to finite performable procedures on integers; when possible, give a computational recipe. This viewpoint motivates the use of interpretations (e.g. Gödel’s Dialectica) to clarify implication and conditionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional statements must have numerical/computational interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop expresses dissatisfaction with standard BHK interpretation of implication and proposes using Gödel’s Dialectica interpretation to offer a more satisfactory computational interpretation of conditional statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or producing constructive work, ensure implications are given a form that yields explicit computational content (algorithms, moduli), not just material implication; consider Dialectica-style readings for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational role of the natural numbers (positive integers primary)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The primary concern of mathematics is number, and this means the positive integers.’ Bishop assigns a foundational role to natural numbers and finite operations on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive practice should ground constructions in operations on the naturals; quantification and mathematical claims should be interpretable in terms of finite procedures relative to the naturals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concerned only with mathematics finite beings can, in principle, carry out
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics should be limited to what a finite being can carry out 'in principle'; classical quantification over infinite domains is assimilated to the doings of an infinite (God-like) mind and is suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid formulations that presuppose ability to perform infinite searches or non-effective methods. Emphasize constructions that, at least in principle, a finite agent could carry out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid free choice sequences and metaphysical speculation about the continuum
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop criticises Brouwer’s free choice sequences as making the continuum 'not well enough defined' and 'so bizarre it becomes unpalatable to mathematicians'; they 'admit no ready numerical interpretation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat theories that introduce free choice sequences or similar abstract devices without numerical/algorithmic interpretation with skepticism; prefer notions of the continuum compatible with explicit numerical meaning and mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve compatibility with classical mathematics when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: A significant characteristic of Bishop's mathematics is full compatibility with classical mathematics: 'every proof in Bishop’s mathematics of a statement is also a classical proof of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing constructive reformulations, aim for approaches that keep the 'spirit' and usability of everyday modern mathematics—so constructive proofs correspond to classical proofs and do not unnecessarily mutilate the mathematical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explicit computational content and single out non-constructive assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive mathematics can express distinctions invisible classically by isolating computational content of theorems and identifying non-constructive assumptions (e.g. implications of the form LPO → T*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing a theorem, show its constructive substitute (T*), exhibit how non-constructive principles enter, and try to produce natural implications that reflect problem structure; avoid hiding non-constructive steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use minimal formalism; enlarge only for genuine mathematical need
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Another important foundational problem is to find a formal system that will efficiently express predictive mathematics. I think we should keep the formalism as primitive as possible, starting with a minimal system and enlarging it only if the enlargement serves a genuine mathematical need.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor small, pragmatically motivated formal systems for expressing constructive content. Use formalization as a tool to clarify numerical meaning, not as an end in itself; avoid heavy formal machinery unless it yields substantive mathematical or interpretative gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization should interact with mathematics to clarify meaning and support computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop came to see formal systems as potentially beneficial if they engage with issues of meaning and predictive embodiment; formalization can help clarify numerical content and aid applications to computing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply formal techniques (e.g. interpretations, type-theoretic frameworks) to make computational meaning explicit and to support mechanization/theorem-proving, but remain critical of purely formal exercises divorced from meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer algorithmic/explicit proofs that construct witnesses step-by-step
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mathematicians (and Bishop) prefer proofs that are algorithmic and explicit: proofs that construct witnesses step-by-step and provide moduli of computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In constructive practice and exposition, favor demonstrations that produce effective constructions; when possible give algorithms or explicit bounds rather than existential nonconstructive arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy must contribute to making mathematics more meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There is only one basic criterion to justify the philosophy of mathematics, and that is, does it contribute to making mathematics more meaningful.’ Philosophy’s role is to clarify meaning, not metaphysical speculation disconnected from practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical reflection should focus on making distinctions of meaning (e.g. between computable and noncomputable integers), informing mathematical methodology and elucidating computational content rather than engaging in remote metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inflexible advocacy; pursue persuasion and dialogue with classical mathematicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop criticizes Brouwer’s inflexible advocacy and emphasizes the need to persuade classical mathematicians by demonstrating the viability and mathematical fruitfulness of constructive methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When promoting constructive approaches, present them in ways accessible to classical mathematicians, show concrete mathematical successes, avoid sectarian rhetoric or 'propaganda' tones that alienate the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative method: use constructive reverse mathematics to relate varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive reverse mathematics is a programme suggested: develop constructive mathematics as a neutral base and obtain other varieties (classical, Brouwerian, Russian) by adding characteristic principles (e.g. excluded middle, axiom of choice, fan theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the method of adding or isolating principles to compare strength and content across varieties; analyze which constructive principles are needed to recover particular classical or Brouwerian results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and make explicit the role of limited omniscience principles (LPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop frames the gap between finite and infinite agents by reference to limited omniscience; LPO (Limited Principle of Omniscience) expresses a minimal omniscience assumed of an infinite agent and marks a boundary between constructive and classical interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating arguments, identify whether they tacitly use principles like LPO. Be explicit about such principles because they signal whether an argument presupposes unlimited search abilities (thus non-constructive commitments).
